title: EF Core query internals -- IQueryable, deferred execution, split queries, compiled queries
exp: Day 6 covered the practical N+1 problem. This day goes into HOW EF Core actually translates your LINQ into SQL, and the specific query-shaping decisions that separate an EF Core novice from someone who can reason about its generated SQL.
pts: `IQueryable<T>` represents an UN-executed query expression tree -- calling .Where(), .Select(), .OrderBy() on it doesn't touch the database, it just builds up the expression tree. The query only executes when you enumerate it: .ToList(), .ToListAsync(), foreach, .First(), .Count(), etc.

This deferred nature means building a query across multiple method calls (a repository pattern chaining .Where() calls, for instance) is fine and even beneficial -- EF Core translates the FULL final expression tree into one SQL query, not one query per method call.

`IEnumerable<T>` vs `IQueryable<T>` is the classic footgun: if you call `.ToList()` too early then continue chaining `.Where()`, the filtering happens in-memory in C# (LINQ-to-Objects) instead of being translated to SQL and executed by the database -- silently pulling far more rows across the wire than necessary.

**Split queries:** by default, EF Core translates multiple `.Include()` calls for collection navigation properties into ONE large SQL query with multiple JOINs, which can produce a Cartesian-product explosion of duplicate row data. `.AsSplitQuery()` tells EF Core to instead issue separate SQL queries per Include, avoiding the row-multiplication at the cost of multiple round-trips.

**Compiled queries** (`EF.CompileAsyncQuery`) pre-compile a LINQ query's translation to SQL once, bypassing the expression-tree-to-SQL translation overhead on every subsequent call -- meaningful for a query executed extremely frequently in a hot path, not worth the added complexity for typical CRUD queries.

Change tracking behavior on a query: EF Core's default tracking query creates a snapshot of every returned entity to detect changes for a future SaveChanges(). This snapshot creation has real CPU/memory cost proportional to the number of entities and properties returned -- `.AsNoTracking()` skips it entirely for read-only scenarios.

`.AsNoTrackingWithIdentityResolution()` is a middle ground: skips full change tracking overhead but still ensures that if the same entity appears multiple times in a result set (via multiple Include paths), you get the same C# object instance rather than duplicate copies -- useful for complex read-only graphs where object identity still matters to your code.

Client-side evaluation warnings: EF Core will throw at runtime (in modern versions) rather than silently falling back to in-memory evaluation if part of your LINQ expression cannot be translated to SQL -- know this is a deliberate design choice to surface performance problems early rather than hide them.
pr: Rewrite a query that calls .ToList() before its final .Where() clause so the filter executes in SQL instead of in-memory

r: Slightly more overhead than plain AsNoTracking
Avoid JOIN row-multiplication from multiple Includes
Only worth it for very hot-path queries

qa.q: What is the classic IQueryable vs IEnumerable footgun in EF Core, and how do you spot it in a code review?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** If .ToList() (or .ToListAsync(), or any other enumeration) is called BEFORE the final .Where()/.OrderBy()/.Select() chain is complete, everything after that point executes as LINQ-to-Objects in memory in C#, not as SQL executed by the database. This silently pulls the entire unfiltered table across the network before applying the filter locally -- correct but catastrophically inefficient on a large table. Spot it in review by checking whether .ToList()/.ToListAsync() appears in the middle of a LINQ chain rather than strictly at the end.

**Under the Hood & Mechanics:** SQL Server query processor constructs a logical tree, estimates cardinality using statistics, and selects physical operators (Nested Loops, Hash Join, or Merge Join) based on cost and sorted indexes.

**Production Failure Mode & Gotcha:** Cartesian products or missing join predicates can cause exponential disk tempdb spilling, memory grant exhaustion, and query timeouts under concurrent load.

**Senior Trade-Off Signal:** Nested loops excel for indexed small lookups; Hash joins handle large unsorted sets at the cost of higher tempdb and memory grant usage.

qa.q: What problem does AsSplitQuery() solve, and what is the trade-off of using it?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** When you Include() multiple collection navigation properties (Orders -> LineItems AND Orders -> StatusHistory, for example), EF Core's default behavior generates one SQL query with multiple JOINs -- but if an order has 5 line items and 3 status history entries, the JOIN produces 15 rows for that one order (a Cartesian product), which EF Core then has to de-duplicate back into the correct object graph client-side. AsSplitQuery() instead issues one SQL query per Include, avoiding the row multiplication, at the cost of multiple round-trips to the database instead of one -- correct choice depends on whether the JOIN explosion or the extra round-trips is the bigger cost for your specific data shape.

**Under the Hood & Mechanics:** SQL Server query processor constructs a logical tree, estimates cardinality using statistics, and selects physical operators (Nested Loops, Hash Join, or Merge Join) based on cost and sorted indexes.

**Production Failure Mode & Gotcha:** Cartesian products or missing join predicates can cause exponential disk tempdb spilling, memory grant exhaustion, and query timeouts under concurrent load.

**Senior Trade-Off Signal:** Nested loops excel for indexed small lookups; Hash joins handle large unsorted sets at the cost of higher tempdb and memory grant usage.

qa.q: When is a compiled query worth the added complexity, and when is it not?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** EF.CompileAsyncQuery pre-compiles the LINQ-to-SQL translation once, avoiding that translation overhead on every subsequent execution -- meaningful for a query that executes extremely frequently (thousands of times per second in a hot path). For typical CRUD queries executed at normal application request rates, the translation overhead EF Core incurs per query is small relative to the actual database round-trip time, so the added code complexity and reduced flexibility of a compiled query usually isn't worth it. Profile first; don't reach for this as a default optimization.

**Under the Hood & Mechanics:** Window functions operate on a set of rows defined by the OVER() clause without collapsing them into a single row, allocating memory segments for frame calculation.

**Production Failure Mode & Gotcha:** Partitioning over non-indexed columns with huge row counts forces expensive Sort operators and TempDB spills in execution plans.

**Senior Trade-Off Signal:** Provides high readability and single-pass analytical aggregation, but can increase RAM grants compared to traditional indexed grouping.

qa.q: Why does modern EF Core throw an exception instead of silently falling back to client-side evaluation for untranslatable LINQ expressions?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** Earlier EF Core versions would silently evaluate any part of a LINQ query that couldn't be translated to SQL by pulling the necessary data into memory and finishing the operation in C# -- which could work correctly but catastrophically underperform on a large table, with no visible warning that this was happening. Modern EF Core throws at runtime instead, forcing the developer to either restructure the query into something translatable or explicitly opt into client evaluation, surfacing a potential performance cliff during development and testing rather than allowing it to silently degrade production performance.

**Under the Hood & Mechanics:** T-SQL engine parses, compiles into execution plans, caches them in the plan cache, and executes via the storage engine (buffer pool & latching).

**Production Failure Mode & Gotcha:** Parameter sniffing and missing stats cause sub-optimal plan compilation, resulting in full table scans and high CPU.

**Senior Trade-Off Signal:** Parameterization improves plan reuse, but recompile hints (OPTION RECOMPILE) may be needed for skewed data distributions.

interviewPlaybook.incidentStory: During a high-concurrency surge, a critical query relying on EF Core query internals -- IQueryable, deferred execution, split queries, compiled queries caused TempDB disk spills and latch contention.
